blocks.label: Definition
blocks.html:
Spearman’s rank correlation coefficient (ρₛ, or rₛ) is Pearson’s r computed on the ranks of the two variables instead of their raw values. With no tied ranks it reduces to

ρₛ = 1 − 6Σd² ÷ [n(n² − 1)]

where d is the difference between a person’s two ranks. Kendall’s tau (τ) counts pairs of people instead:

τ = (C − D) ÷ [n(n − 1)/2]

where C is the number of concordant pairs (the person higher on X is also higher on Y) and D the number of discordant pairs (Kendall, 1938). Both measure a monotonic relationship and lie between −1 and +1.

blocks.label: Simplified Explanation
blocks.html:
Recall that the Mann–Whitney test (§10.2) replaces values by ranks. Spearman’s coefficient does the same for correlation. Ranks ignore how far apart the values are, so an outlier can do no more than take the top rank, and a curved but steadily rising relationship ranks perfectly.

Kendall’s τ asks a plainer question. Take every possible pair of people. Does the taller of the two also weigh more? τ and ρₛ are on different scales, so a τ from one study cannot be set beside a ρₛ from another. τ has a direct reading: the proportion of agreeing pairs minus the proportion of disagreeing pairs.

blocks.label: Illustration / Example
blocks.html: The Kuppuswamy socioeconomic scale and a health literacy score are both ordinal (recall §1.1.2). Their intervals are not equal, so Pearson’s r is not appropriate. Rank both and use ρₛ or τ.

blocks.label: Worked Calculation
blocks.html:
The same eight children as in §11.2:

Child 1 2 3 4 5 6 7 8
Height rank 3 2 7 1 6 8 4 5
Weight rank 4 1 8 2 6 7 3 5
d −1 1 −1 −1 0 1 1 0
d² 1 1 1 1 0 1 1 0
  1. Σd² = 6; n = 8, so n(n² − 1) = 8 × 63 = 504.
  2. ρₛ = 1 − (6 × 6) ÷ 504 = 1 − 0.071 = 0.93.
  3. Kendall: there are 8 × 7 ÷ 2 = 28 pairs of children. Checking each pair, 25 are concordant and 3 discordant (children 1 and 7, 2 and 4, 3 and 6: in each pair the taller child is the lighter one).
  4. τ = (25 − 3) ÷ 28 = 0.79.

For all 100 children, age against weight gives ρₛ = 0.83 and τ = 0.66, close to Pearson’s 0.82 because the relationship is close to linear and has no extreme outliers.

blocks.label: In R (optional)
blocks.html:
cl <- read.csv("data/clinic_children.csv")
cor.test(cl$age_months, cl$weight_kg, method = "spearman",
         exact = FALSE)
cor.test(cl$age_months, cl$weight_kg, method = "kendall",
         exact = FALSE)
    Spearman's rank correlation rho
...
S = 28518, p-value < 2.2e-16
sample estimates:
     rho 
0.828872 

    Kendall's rank correlation tau
...
z = 9.3613, p-value < 2.2e-16
sample estimates:
      tau 
0.6550698

ρₛ = 0.83 and τ = 0.66. Ages are recorded in whole months, so many children share a rank; exact = FALSE asks for the large-sample p-values, which handle ties. R’s τ with ties is the tie-corrected version (tau-b).

points.html: Use a rank coefficient when at least one variable is ordinal, when the relationship is monotonic but curved, or when outliers make r unreliable (Schober et al., 2018).
The d² formula is exact only without ties. With ties, compute Pearson’s r on the ranks (software such as R does this).
When the data are Normal and linear, rank coefficients have somewhat less power than r, the same trade-off as between parametric and non-parametric tests (recall §10.1).
